failures.rule: [1,2,3,,] is explicitly called invalid because it has two trailing commas
[,1,2,3] is explicitly called invalid because it has an initial comma
[1,,2,3] is explicitly called invalid because it has two commas in a row
these same comma rules apply to fields in objects, so two commas in a row between fields is invalid just as in an array
an initial comma is invalid in an object, the implicit root included
the array comma rules apply to object fields: two trailing commas are invalid
the array comma rules apply to object fields: an initial comma is invalid
U+00A0 is a Zs space and so whitespace in HOCON; between two list substitutions it is ignored (lightbend/config#862 review)
the BOM must be treated as whitespace, so between two list substitutions it is ignored

the spec's own example: an intermediate non-object value hides earlier object values because merging is done in pairs, so when 42 is paired with { y : 2 } it simply wins and loses all information about what it overrode, and the two objects are never merged
the spec's re-ordered example: with the non-object 42 moved to the lowest priority the two objects are adjacent, so they merge to { a : { x : 1, y : 2 } }

merging is always done two values at a time: the scalar replaces the first object (non-object always wins), then the second object replaces the scalar (no merging, object is the new value), so the two objects never see each other

v's value is a merge whose top is an object and whose null sits further down, under nested; that null is still v.nested's merge instruction, so a.nested keeps helper (lightbend/config#864 review, round 3)
a string concatenation is a non-object value, so the later object replaces it rather than merging with it
the number cuts the merge off from anything before it; the empty object after it and the object after that still merge, and the empty one contributes nothing
exactly ns, nano, nanos, nanosecond, nanoseconds are the supported unit strings for nanoseconds
exactly us, micro, micros, microsecond, microseconds are the supported unit strings for microseconds
exactly ms, milli, millis, millisecond, milliseconds are the supported unit strings for milliseconds
exactly s, second, seconds are the supported unit strings for seconds
exactly m, minute, minutes are the supported unit strings for minutes
exactly h, hour, hours are the supported unit strings for hours
exactly d, day, days are the supported unit strings for days in the duration format

a name without an extension is a basename: all of base.properties, base.json and base.conf exist, so all three are loaded and merged, properties first and HOCON last, so the .conf value wins where they overlap
a basename with only base.conf present loads just that file
a basename with only base.properties present loads it as Java properties, whose values are all strings

a file named .json is in JSON format, and an unquoted value is not JSON. typesafe/config parses a .json named outright with the HOCON parser, so the file is accepted; the same file found through a basename is rejected

a file named .properties is in Java properties format, where the first = separates key from value and values are strings. typesafe/config parses a .properties named outright with the HOCON parser and fails on the second =; the same file found through a basename is read as properties

in a properties file a dotted key is a path, so a.b and a.c build an object at a; the spec's Java properties mapping says the object must always win when a key is both a value and a parent, whatever the order; values are strings
a .json file found through a basename is parsed as JSON and contributes its object
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; an unquoted value is a HOCON extension, not JSON
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; ${} is a HOCON extension, not JSON
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON has no trailing commas
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; the spec's own footing is that duplicate keys are invalid JSON (L194-195), so the second a is an error rather than an override
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON separates array elements with commas only; whitespace does not concatenate or separate
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; an empty document is not JSON, although it is an empty HOCON object
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON document included here must be an object; a bare number is neither an object nor valid as an included root
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON key is a quoted string; a number cannot be a key
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; in JSON a newline between fields does not stand in for the comma
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON key is a plain string, not a path expression, so a.b stays a single key
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON forbids a leading zero on a number. typesafe/config reads 01 as 1, the same leniency it shows in HOCON
a substitution in an included file must be fixed up to be relative to the app's configuration root, so ${x} in a file included at key a becomes ${a.x}
substitution happens after parsing the whole configuration, so the ${x} fixed up to ${a.x} evaluates to the root's later redefinition 42 rather than the included file's 10
substitutions in included files are looked up first relative to the root of the included file and only second relative to the root of the including configuration, so a.x wins over x
the fix-up is relative to the app's configuration root, so ${x} in a file included at b inside a file included at a becomes ${a.b.x}
an undefined optional that would override keeps the previous value, so common.x.y is 9 and found at the fixed-up path; the original path is not consulted
an object merged with a substitution in the included file keeps working after the fix-up, whichever of the two is on top: q is found at p.q
a.x is present, set to null, so the lookup at the fixed-up path succeeds and the original path x is not consulted
the string inside url() is interpreted as a URL, and x.conf has no scheme, so it is not one
failures.open_question: the spec says only that the string inside url() is interpreted as a URL; it does not say whether a string that is not a URL is an error or an unresolvable, hence ignorable, resource. typesafe/config rejects it

failures.rule: a classpath() include names a resource; when it does not exist the include is ignored like any other missing include, and an implementation without a classpath has nothing to find there either
any amount of whitespace, newlines included, may stand between include and the resource name
an unquoted include at the start of a key is never a key; followed by a separator instead of a quoted name it is an include with an invalid argument
the separator may be omitted before {, and the spec does not say whether a newline may stand between the key and the brace; typesafe/config and pyhocon accept it, hocon-rs rejects it
failures.open_question: the spec is silent on a newline between a key and its brace; implementations disagree

failures.rule: the [] suffix collects CONFORMANCE_LIST_0, CONFORMANCE_LIST_1, ... until an index is missing, into a list of strings. typesafe/config 1.4.5 predates the syntax and rejects the path
indices are collected from 0 until one is missing, so with _0 and _2 set the list holds only the first; typesafe/config 1.4.5 predates the syntax
an element taken from the environment is a string, so 1 stays "1"; typesafe/config 1.4.5 predates the syntax
the conversion should be done in a concatenation when a list is expected and an object with numeric keys is found, so the trailing object concatenates onto the array as elements x, y
the conversion should ignore any keys which do not parse as positive integers, so key "foo" is dropped and only "0" contributes to the resulting array

the conversion should sort by the integer value of each key and then build the array; missing indices such as "1" are eliminated rather than left as gaps, so keys "0" and "2" become a two-element array
the conversion ignores any keys which do not parse as positive integers, and "-1" is not a positive integer, so it is dropped and only key "0" contributes
foo.bar."hello.world" is a path with three elements: foo, bar, and hello.world, since unquoted dots are path separators but a quoted dot is not
foo followed by quoted "10.0" is an unquoted then a quoted string which concatenate, giving a single-element path
a path element that is an empty string must be quoted; a."".b is a valid three-element path whose middle element is the empty string
an unquoted empty path element is invalid, so a..b must generate an error
a path that starts with a dot is invalid and should generate an error
a path that ends with a dot is invalid and should generate an error

an unquoted empty path element is invalid in a substitution just as in a key, so ${a..b} must generate an error rather than collapsing to ${a.b} (a.b is defined so a lenient implementation would produce a value and fail)

the unquoted string include may not begin a path expression in a key: where an object key is expected, include is not read as a key at all and must be followed by a quoted resource name, so include.foo is an error. typesafe/config recognises the keyword only as a bare include token -- include.foo tokenizes as one unquoted string, so it is accepted as the path include.foo, while include = 42 is rejected under the very rule the spec states.
only the unquoted string include that begins a path expression in a key is special: include later in a key (foo.include) and a quoted "include" beginning one are ordinary path elements
exactly d, day, days are the supported unit strings for days in the period format
exactly w, week, weeks are the supported unit strings for weeks
exactly m, mo, month, months are the supported unit strings for months
the spec notes that getTemporal() callers should prefer mo over m for months, since m is also the duration unit for minutes and getTemporal() may return either a Duration or a Period
a += b transforms into a = ${?a} [b], and because the fallback is optional (${?a} not ${a}) this is legal even as the first mention of a in the file
+= appends an element to a previous array
if the previous value was not an array, += results in an error just as the long form a = ${?a} [b] would with a non-array a
each += appends to the value the previous line left, so two of them append two elements
inside an object, += desugars to a self-reference by the field's full path o.a; the appended element may itself be a substitution
b has no previous value, so b += 1 is b = ${?b} [1] with the optional part undefined: [1]. typesafe/config refuses += inside a list because its desugared path cannot name a list element
the self-reference += desugars to uses the full path of the field, o.p.a, even when the enclosing key was written as the path o.p

l += v is l = ${?l} [v]; the appended object holds a merge of an object and a substitution, which resolves inside the new list. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) for the same reason as array-and-object-concatenation/018

this case has undefined behavior depending on resolution order: implementations are allowed to set both a and b to 1, both to 2, or to error, but must set both to the same value because substitutions are memoized by instance, so a and b must never diverge (e.g. a=1,b=2 is not permitted)
failures.open_question: the spec allows both fields to be 1, both 2, or an error (L875-877); only 'the same value' is required, which one expected tree cannot express. typesafe/config itself gives 1 or 2 depending on key order

failures.rule: ${replacement} resolves to 42, a non-object, so the earlier object is hidden and never evaluated -- as with the literal in 005. typesafe/config 1.4.5 evaluates it; 1.4.9 and later do not
a string concatenation is a non-object too, so it hides the earlier object. typesafe/config 1.4.5 evaluates it; 1.4.9 and later do not
w += 1 is w = ${?w} [1], which reads the earlier list, so ${does-not-exist} is evaluated: an error
a genuine cycle is an error for required substitutions; with the optional syntax it is a missing value, so neither field is created

every power-of-2 suffix and its long forms name the same unit family; one table, one rule. The E and e forms are quoted because an unquoted 5E is a number token that is not a number (see unquoted-strings/022)
true and false become the strings "true" and "false" when they participate in a concatenation
null becomes the string "null" when it participates in a concatenation
false becomes the string "false" in a concatenation, as true does
setting a key to null in the configuration explicitly blocks looking that substitution up in the environment, so ${CONFORMANCE_X} resolves to null even though the variable is set
a substitution is replaced with any value type and, when it is the only part of a value, the type is preserved: here string, true, false and null stay what they were rather than becoming strings

a substitution is undefined only if it does not match any value present in the configuration, and null is among the value types a substitution is replaced with, so ${?a} with a = null is defined: the field is created with null rather than omitted
the path inside ${} has the syntax of an object key, and whitespace before the first and after the last element of a key is discarded, so ${ b } is ${b}
the same path with the optional form: undefined, so the field is not created
an empty path element is legal when quoted, in a substitution as in a key

a path names object fields only, so b.0 does not reach into the list b even though it has an element at index 0; the optional substitution is undefined and a is not created. The list is still unresolved when the lookup happens, which is what makes an implementation look inside it
only whitespace before the ? is forbidden; after it the path follows and its leading whitespace is discarded as in any key

${?x}42 is a concatenation of two parts, so the value is a string: the undefined optional becomes empty and the number keeps its written form. The spec states the empty-string rule for a concatenation 'with another string', so this row extends it to a number; typesafe/config instead drops the undefined part and keeps the lone number as a number
quoted strings are in the same format as JSON strings, so JSON escapes like \n, \t, \", \\ and \u unicode escapes are honored

allowed number formats match JSON, and JSON forbids a zero followed by further digits; the initial number character plus the valid-in-JSON number characters after it must be parsed as a number value, so the whole token 01 has to be a number and is not one, with no fallback offered. typesafe/config parses it leniently as the number 1.

allowed number formats match JSON, and JSON requires a digit before the decimal point, so -.33 is a number token that is not a valid number. typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -0.33; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) reads it as the unquoted string "-.33", like .33 -- still accepted, still not the error the hyphen rule asks for

the same JSON rule with an exponent: -.33e+1 has no integer part. typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -3.3; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) rejects it, on the reserved +
JSON requires a digit after the decimal point; 1. is a number token that is not a valid number. typesafe/config reads it as 1, and lightbend/config#861 leaves it so on purpose
the same rule with an exponent after the dot; typesafe/config reads it as -1000 (named out of scope in lightbend/config#861)
JSON forbids leading zeros after the minus sign as well; typesafe/config reads it as -33 (named out of scope in lightbend/config#861)
the JSON escapes \/ \b \f and \r are valid in a quoted string and mean slash, backspace, form feed and carriage return
only the JSON escape sequences exist; \q is not one of them, so the string is invalid
\u must be followed by exactly four hex digits; zzzz are not hex digits
a raw tab is a control character too, so it must be written as \t inside quotes
the file is UTF-8, so a multi-byte sequence is one character
JSON writes a character outside the BMP as two \u escapes forming a surrogate pair, which decode to one character
a string value with a unit name has that name specify the value's interpretation
the two-character string '//' starts a comment, ending the unquoted string before it even mid-token
backslash is a forbidden character, and unquoted strings support no escaping at all, so a literal backslash requires a quoted string instead

an unquoted string may not begin with a hyphen, and the initial number character plus any valid-in-JSON number characters that follow must be parsed as a number value -- here that is the lone '-', which is not a number. typesafe/config falls back to unquoted text and yields the string '-foo', the same leniency it shows for '1e'.
quoted JSON strings may not contain control characters, per the JSON spec, unlike unquoted strings
only 0-9 and - begin a number, so .33 is an ordinary unquoted string -- the reading lightbend/config#861 extends to -.33
1+2 begins like a number and is not one; + is a forbidden character, so the token cannot fall back to an unquoted string either
1e begins with a digit, so the run of number characters 1e must be parsed as a number, and it is not one; typesafe/config falls back to the unquoted string "1e", the same leniency it shows for -foo
a nonbreaking space (0x00A0) is a Unicode Zs separator and must be treated as whitespace
the BOM (0xFEFF) must be treated as whitespace, not as part of the key
vertical tab (0x000B) and form feed (0x000C) are whitespace characters
the spec names figure space (0x2007) and narrow no-break space (0x202F) explicitly among the nonbreaking spaces treated as whitespace
a lone carriage return is whitespace but not a newline, so 1 b concatenates and the second = is a stray token
U+2028 around the separator is whitespace, not part of the key or the value
the file, group, record and unit separators 0x1C-0x1F are whitespace around keys and separators
the ideographic space U+3000 is a Zs space separator and so whitespace, like every member of the category
the BOM is whitespace wherever it appears, not only as a file-start marker
